chapter_note: This chapter is almost entirely hagiographic-biographical narrative (Mani’s journeys, summons by Shapur, opposition by rulers/sects) framed as dialogue, with a late Christian overlay via the Johannine dictum about the world loving darkness. The second half drifts into explicit exhortation/prayer for the community (holy church), but there is no recoverable systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential teaching substrate here.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic travel notice with reverential titles (“our master… light enlightener”) and court setting; narrative frame rather than cosmological exposition.
Biographical repetition of Shapur’s summons; “proclaimed… the word of God” as narrative report, not a systematic teaching layer.
Brief continuation of the court-journey narrative (third summons); no doctrinal structure.
Dialogue set-up with named disciple and petition for “two Manis”; hagiographic scene construction and honorific address.
Self-referential apostolic speech (“I, a single Mani, came to the world…”). This is biographical/apologetic voice, not impersonal cosmological mapping.
Continuation of first-person apologetic about not being permitted to speak; mission narrative rather than substrate teaching.
Explicit Johannine overlay (“the world loves the darkness… hates the light… works are evil” = Jn 3 theme); entered via Gospel tradition rather than core Manichaean cosmological exposition.
Disciple’s response/question in the dialogue; fragmentary but functions as conversational scaffolding.
Missionary travel narrative (sea voyage, India, stirring the land); historical/biographical reporting.
First-person complaint about losing freedom to speak; still mission narrative.
Returns to the Johannine maxim (“world loves darkness… hates light…”), alongside political titles; the Gospel-derived line marks Christian overlay even though the setting is India.
Itinerary (India → Persia) with proclamation to “powers… authorities… holders of authority”; narrative rhetoric, not a closed cosmological degree-structure.
Fragmentary reassurance invoking the Father’s help; devotional/biographical tone.
Rhetorical contrast: land tolerates kings but not Mani’s truth; repeated political catalogue is characteristic of the travel-apologia layer.

Mission report with dualistic slogans (“separated the light from the darkness… life from death”), but used as a summary of preaching in a travel narrative and extended into “commandments”; not an impersonal cosmos→cosmos mapping sequence.
Opposition narrative involving “ruling-power” and “swarm of demons,” but still framed as persecution while preaching; no systematic correspondential architecture.
Travel to Babylon/Assyrian cities; proclamation report with the same preaching-summary rhetoric.
Persecution scene (judges, rulers) plus devotional aside about the Father’s protection; the address “as you yourselves see” remains within the biographical-hagiographic register.
Rhetorical “See now” plus political titles; continues the travel-contrast motif (lands accept rulers but reject his truth).
Journey to Medes/Parthians; metaphor (“played the harp of wisdom”) serves narrative flourish, not a structured correspondential teaching unit.
Explicit dialogue attribution (“Then the apostle speaks…”) and triumphal self-presentation (“planted… sown seed of life”); hagiographic framing rather than substrate exposition.
Continuation of the ‘one vs two Manis’ rhetorical argument; no cosmological mechanism taught.
Metaphorical self-description (walking on tip-toes) in mission context; biographical lament style.
Direct exhortation to the audience (“All of you, pray to God…”) and explicit institutional marker “holy church”; community-focused application layer.
Second-person beatitude/exhortation (“blessed are you… make yourselves strong…”)—application voice aimed at the hearers rather than cosmological description.
Hagiographic response of the disciple with blessing formulas, familial honorifics (“our father”), and encomium; functions as chapter closure frame.
